pedagogy.summary: Having seen that tiling a rectangle equals the product of its side lengths, children now compute area directly by multiplying the side lengths (7 cm × 9 cm = 63 cm²) and work the relationship backwards — representing a whole-number product as a rectangle of that area. The multiplication carries meaning from the array (squares in a row × rows), and the answer is in square units.
bestPractices: Compute area as side × side, keeping the array meaning (one side = squares in a row, the other = number of rows) in view.
Insist on square units in the answer (cm², m²), tying the unit back to unit squares.
Work the reverse: given an area like 36 square units, find rectangles that have it (factor pairs) and label their sides.
Use real contexts (a garden 8 m by 5 m) so the multiplication solves a problem.
Contrast multiplying for area with adding for perimeter so the two are not conflated.
keyRepresentations: A rectangle labelled 7 cm × 9 cm with area 63 cm²
An area model linking multiplication to a rectangle of squares
Several rectangles all of area 36 (2×18, 3×12, 4×9, 6×6) with sides labelled
commonMisconceptions: Adds the side lengths (perimeter) instead of multiplying for area.
Gives the answer in linear units (cm) rather than square units (cm²).
Cannot reverse the relationship — struggles to draw a rectangle of a given area or to find its factor-pair sides.
Multiplies unrelated numbers or applies l×w to a non-rectangle.

learn.summary: Children compute the area of a rectangle by multiplying its side lengths (7 cm × 9 cm = 63 cm²), keeping the array meaning in view (squares in a row × number of rows) and answering in square units. They also work the relationship backwards: given a target area such as 36 square units, they construct rectangles whose side lengths multiply to that area (2×18, 3×12, 4×9, 6×6) and label the sides. Multiplying for area is explicitly contrasted with adding for perimeter so the two measures are not conflated.

activities.title: Build and compute: side × side = area
feedback: If a learner adds the sides (7 + 9 = 16), return to the tiled array: area is rows of squares, so it is squares-in-a-row × rows. Re-derive 7 × 9 from the tiling before using the formula.
If the number is right but the unit is linear (63 cm), tie the unit to the unit square: each tile is 1 cm², so the count is in square centimetres — always write the squared unit.

For the garden, if a learner answers 13, ask 'what did 8 + 5 actually measure?' (the length of two touching sides, which is only half the distance around: the perimeter is 8 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 26 m) to separate edge lengths from the surface covered (8 × 5 = 40 m²).
activities.rationale: Multiplying side lengths to find rectangle area rests on understanding area as covering with unit squares arranged in rows; keeping the array meaning visible lets the formula carry the counting meaning, and insisting on square units guards against the common linear-unit slip.
sourceClaims: Students learn to multiply length measurements to find the area of a rectangular region, understanding this as a multiplicative relationship of the number of square units in a row and the number of rows; they explain why multiplying the side lengths gives the same area as counting the tiles, and represent whole-number products as rectangular areas (3.MD.7).
Year 4 pupils find the area of rectilinear shapes by counting squares and multiply side lengths to find areas of rectangles.
learnerActions: Choose two side lengths for a rectangle (e.g. 7 and 9) and draw it on squared paper or with a grid overlay.
Count the squares as rows of squares (squares-in-a-row × number of rows) and confirm this equals multiplying the side lengths: 7 × 9 = 63.
Write the answer with square units: 63 cm².
Change one side (e.g. 7 → 8) and recompute, noticing the rectangle re-tiles and the area becomes 8 × 9 = 72 cm².
Solve a real context: a garden 8 m by 5 m — find its area (8 × 5 = 40 m²).
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying the two side lengths gives the same total as counting all the unit squares, because the rectangle is a number of equal rows; the result is measured in square units.

activities.title: Reverse the relationship: many rectangles, one area
feedback: If a learner draws a rectangle that is not 36 (e.g. sides that don't multiply to 36), find factor pairs of 36 together and match each pair to a rectangle, using the grid to verify.
If a learner finds only one option and stops, prompt systematically: 'Does 2 divide 36? 3? 4? 6?' to surface more factor pairs (and note 1×36 is also valid).
Confirm 6×6 counts as a valid rectangle (a square) with area 36.
activities.rationale: Representing a whole-number product as a rectangular area and finding factor-pair sides deepens the product–area link and addresses the common difficulty of reversing the relationship.
sourceClaims: Students learn to multiply length measurements to find the area of a rectangular region, understanding this as a multiplicative relationship of the number of square units in a row and the number of rows; they explain why multiplying the side lengths gives the same area as counting the tiles, and represent whole-number products as rectangular areas (3.MD.7).
learnerActions: Given a fixed area of 36 square units, find rectangles whose sides multiply to 36 and draw each, labelling the sides.
List the factor pairs discovered: 2×18, 3×12, 4×9, 6×6 — all have area 36 (and 1×36 is also valid).
Check each rectangle against a grid to confirm it really covers 36 squares.
State what stays the same across all of them (the product/area = 36) and what changes (the shape).
activities.intendedInsight: One area can be made by many different rectangles; it is the product of the side lengths, not the shape, that is fixed.

activities.title: Area versus perimeter: surface versus edge
feedback: If a learner uses the perimeter value as the area, ask them to shade the surface and trace the edge separately so the two quantities are visibly different.
Reinforce that area answers end in square units (cm², m²) while perimeter answers end in linear units (cm, m).
activities.rationale: Contrasting the two measures directly addresses the frequent misconception of adding side lengths when area is required and of mislabelling units; the distinction between surface (square units) and distance around (linear units) must be maintained.
sourceClaims: Area formulas must rest on a firm conceptual foundation about what area is (covering with unit squares); the distinction between area (surface, square units) and perimeter (distance around, linear units) must be maintained, guarding against adding side lengths when area is required.
learnerActions: For a 7 × 9 rectangle, work out both the area (multiply: 63 cm²) and the perimeter (add the sides around: 7 + 9 + 7 + 9 = 32 cm).
Say in words what each measures: area covers the surface in square units; perimeter is the distance around in linear units.
Given a mixed set of problems, decide for each whether to multiply (area) or add the edges (perimeter) and justify the choice.
Explain why a friend who did 8 + 5 = 13 for the garden's area has found something other than the area.
activities.intendedInsight: Area (surface, square units) and perimeter (distance around, linear units) are different measures computed differently; multiplying finds area, adding the edges finds perimeter.

activities.title: Check your understanding: compute, select, and label units
feedback: If a distractor equal to the perimeter is chosen, revisit the area-versus-perimeter contrast so the surface (multiply) and the edge (add) are kept distinct.
If the unit is linear, link back to the unit square (1 cm² per tile).
For wrong products, re-derive the multiplication from the array of rows.
activities.rationale: Targeted recognition and short-answer items can surface the add-vs-multiply error and the unit error during practice; recognition alone does not, however, elicit independent construction of a rectangle of a given area (see constraints), so pair these with open drawing/building tasks.
learnerActions: Compute the area of a given rectangle and write it with correct square units (fill-in or short answer).
From several rectangles, select the one(s) with area 36, including a distractor whose perimeter is 36 (an 'add the sides' trap) but whose area is not 36.
Choose the correct unit for an area (cm vs cm²) and explain why.
Solve a word problem: a garden 8 m by 5 m — give the area with units (40 m²).
activities.intendedInsight: Applying area-as-product fluently means multiplying (not adding), using square units, and recognising correct rectangles for a target area.

constraints: Keep the array meaning in view: one side = squares in a row, the other = number of rows; the formula should carry the counting meaning, not replace it.
Always require square units (cm², m²) in area answers, tied back to the unit square.

A static labelled rectangle (e.g. '7 cm × 9 cm, area 63 cm²') is a useful reference for illustrating one calculation, but on its own it cannot have the learner compute across varied cases or perform the reverse construction; pair it with tasks where the learner computes and builds.

Recognition/selection items (choosing which rectangle has area 36, choosing cm vs cm²) can check understanding during teaching, but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of a rectangle of a given area; include open drawing/building tasks for that objective.
This content is for planar rectangular area; avoid presenting it with volume/solid contexts that could confuse area with volume.

Interactive supports — e.g. a live-updating 'l × w = area' label, an optional unit-square grid overlay, a reverse mode that fixes the area while the learner adjusts dimensions, and a perimeter toggle — are helpful optional illustrations of the mechanism, not required mechanisms; the same learning can be done on squared paper.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 7×9=63 ✓; 8×9=72 ✓; 8×5=40 ✓; perimeter of 7×9 = 2(7+9)=32 ✓; factor pairs of 36 used (2×18, 3×12, 4×9, 6×6) all multiply to 36 ✓, and 6×6 is a square with area 36 ✓ (1×36 also valid). The original '7 + 9 = 16' and the '32' perimeter value are retained only as described error patterns/distractors, not as correct answers.
The activity-4 distractor was clarified to a rectangle whose perimeter (not sum of two sides) equals 36, so that the action and its feedback refer to the same area-vs-perimeter trap.

The parentTitle in the source row reads 'Understanding angles (age 8+)', which does not match this area/measurement microtopic; flagged as a likely metadata mismatch. Not changed here (only learning guidance is editable), but should be reviewed.
The UK National Curriculum source is marked verified:false in the row; its claim is cited but its verification status is unconfirmed.

Legacy entries asserted that 3D 'risks confusing it with volume' and that area is 'not a dialogue'; these were softened to narrowly scoped constraints/affordances rather than universal claims about what a medium can or cannot teach.

probeDeeper: Why do you multiply the two sides rather than add them to get the area?
You got 63 — 63 what? Why is the unit 'square centimetres'?
Can you draw a different rectangle that also has an area of 36? How many can you find?
Your friend did 8 + 5 = 13 for the garden — what did they actually work out?
assess.correctAnswer: The child multiplies the side lengths (7×9 = 63 cm²; 8×5 = 40 m²), states the answer in square units, and for the reverse task draws a valid rectangle whose sides multiply to 36 (e.g. 4×9 or 6×6) with sides labelled.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds the side lengths instead of multiplying: gives 7 + 9 = 16 (or a perimeter) as the area.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the tiled array — the area is rows of squares, so it is squares-in-a-row × rows; re-derive 7×9 from tiling before using the formula.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 7 + 9, or answers 16 or 32; treats area like distance around.

errorPatterns.pattern: Linear units instead of square units: computes 63 but labels it '63 cm' rather than '63 cm²'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Tie the unit to the unit square — each tile is 1 cm², so the count is in square centimetres; always write the squared unit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct number, wrong unit — no 'square' in the unit for an area.

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot reverse: struggles to draw a rectangle of a given area or to find factor-pair sides, giving a shape whose sides don't multiply to the target.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Find factor pairs of the area together (2×18, 3×12, 4×9, 6×6) and match each to a rectangle; use the grid to check.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 'area 36', draws a rectangle that isn't 36, or can only think of one option and gets stuck.

responseLevels.gap: Adds the sides (perimeter), or gives linear units, or cannot construct a rectangle of a given area.
responseLevels.full: Computes area as the product of the side lengths in square units, solves area word problems, and reverses the relationship to draw and label rectangles of a given area.
responseLevels.partial: Multiplies the sides correctly for a given rectangle but slips on units (cm not cm²) or cannot reliably reverse to build a target area.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Pose three tasks: 'Find the area of a 7 cm by 9 cm rectangle'; 'Draw a rectangle with an area of 36 square units and label its sides'; and 'A garden is 8 m by 5 m — what is its area?' Watch whether they multiply (not add) the sides, whether they use square units, and whether they can reverse the relationship to construct a given area.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands area-as-product multiplies and gives square units, and can build a rectangle of a target area; a child who does not adds the sides (perimeter), gives linear units, or cannot reverse to find factor-pair sides — each visible in the work.
